Appendix A — the score, in detail

The one object that ties code length, estimation and the Fisher matrix together.

The score is the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameters:

In words: for this dataset, the score says which way to nudge each parameter to make the data more likely, and how strongly. In the compression language of §9, it is how much the code length changes when you change the cosmology — a parameter the data barely constrains is one the optimal code hardly notices.

Two properties that do all the work

(1) At the true parameters the score averages to zero. Differentiating the normalisation :

So on average the fit is already optimal — there is no systematic direction to move.

(2) Its covariance is the Fisher matrix. Differentiating once more gives the two equivalent forms used in §9:

So the Fisher information is literally how much the score jitters from dataset to dataset: a lot of jitter means the data is very sensitive to the parameter, hence tight error bars ().

Why the score is central to inference and compression

Estimation
the maximum-likelihood estimate solves ; a Newton–Raphson step towards it uses the Fisher matrix as the curvature, .
Compression
score compression (generalized MOPED [6]) takes the score at a fiducial model as the compressed summary, — one number per parameter that carries all the Fisher information the full dataset had.
SBI
these score summaries are the natural input to simulation-based inference — a low-dimensional, information-rich code the posterior is then learned over.

Worked example: the score is the matched filter

Take Gaussian data with covariance , so . The score is

Setting gives the best-fit amplitude; evaluated at the fiducial it is the compressed summary — exactly the matched filter — and its Fisher information is , the same as the full dataset's. The score is the matched filter a physicist already trusts, written in one line.

Weak lensing. If you have a differentiable forward model or a flow that returns for a convergence map, automatic differentiation hands you the score directly — and that score, one number per cosmological parameter, is the optimal compression of the whole map for inference. It is the thread connecting the matched filter, MOPED, and modern field-level inference into a single idea.

Appendix B — how an autoencoder works, by hand

Two tiny examples you can check with a pen: watch the numbers flow through encode → code → decode.

Strip an autoencoder to its bones. The encoder turns the input into a short code, the decoder turns the code back into data:

trained to make . If we drop the nonlinearity and the biases and tie the weights (), everything becomes arithmetic you can do by hand — and the result is exactly PCA (§3, §5). Let us trace one.

B.1 — A linear autoencoder, 4 → 1 → 4

Take a single bottleneck unit with weight vector (note ). This unit is a feature detector: it responds to "first half high, second half low". Feed it .

Encode
the code is one dot product:
Decode
rebuild by scaling the detector:
Error

Where the nonlinearity comes in

Give the encoder two units, and , each followed by a ReLU . For our : , . The ReLU has gated the two directions — only one fires — so the decoder can treat "pattern present" and "pattern absent" differently. Stack a few such gated layers and the code becomes a curved coordinate on the data, which is why the nonlinear autoencoder in §5 could follow the arc that linear PCA could not.

B.2 — A 2D image, 16 → 2 → 16

Exactly the same mechanism works on an image; the bottleneck units just become little stencils. Take the 4×4 image below, and two detectors: measures left–right contrast, measures top–bottom contrast (each is , unit norm). The two code numbers are the elementwise products summed over the image,

and the reconstruction is just the two stencils added back in those amounts, .

What this teaches

An autoencoder's code numbers are just measurements of the data against learned templates, and reconstruction is a weighted sum of those templates. Compression is lossless exactly when the data lives in the span of the templates; a richer image — say, with a single bright pixel the two global stencils cannot represent — would leave that detail in a non-zero residual, which is the information thrown away. You buy back that detail by adding more bottleneck units (more stencils) or, more powerfully, by adding nonlinearity so the templates can bend. In the linear case the best possible stencils are precisely the PCA / KL modes of §3; training an autoencoder is how it learns good stencils from data rather than being handed them.

Appendix C — reconstruction vs realization

Do you get the same sky back, or a new one with the same statistics? It depends on phases.

A natural worry: when you encode a field and decode it, is the output the same field, degraded — or a fresh random realization that merely looks similar? The answer is a clean dichotomy, and the whole thing turns on Fourier phases.

Write any field as a sum of Fourier modes, each with an amplitude and a phase:

The crucial fact: the power spectrum depends only on the amplitudes , not on the phases . The phases carry the morphology — where the peaks sit, how filaments align, whether the one-point distribution is skewed. This splits the two operations cleanly:

Reconstruction
a deterministic autoencoder returns — it keeps the amplitudes and the phases of the modes it retained, and loses the rest. You get the same sky, degraded: structures in the same places, but blurred. (An MSE-trained decoder outputs the conditional mean , which is why it comes out smoothed.)
Realization
a generative model that you sample keeps the amplitudes (the learned and higher-order statistics) but draws new phases. You get a different sky from the same ensemble: same statistics, new morphology.

C.1 — one Fourier mode (one wavelength)

Take the simplest field, a single mode . Its only Fourier coefficient sits at with . A new realization redraws its phase: — i.e. the same wave, shifted. The power spectrum is unchanged (phase drops out of ). For one mode a realization is literally a translation; nothing statistical has changed at all.

C.2 — two Fourier modes (one + two wavelengths)

Now add a second mode, . The power spectrum is two spikes, and , and — again — it does not depend on . But the shape now does: the relative phase decides whether the two waves add into a sharp peak or a gentle undulation. So new random phases give a genuinely different-looking field with the same power spectrum.

This is where non-Gaussianity lives

For a Gaussian field the phases are independent and uniformly random, so a power-spectrum description is complete. Non-Gaussianity is phase correlation — the modes conspire (as in the two-mode shape above) to build peaks and filaments. A deterministic reconstruction keeps those phase correlations (same morphology); a Gaussian resample destroys them (right power spectrum, wrong, feature-less sky). Quantifying exactly these phase correlations is the subject of my own phase-statistics work — this appendix is that distinction in miniature.

C.3 — a 2D log-normal sky: statistics stay, the sky changes

Now the real case. I took a non-Gaussian (log-normal) convergence field, used its generator (draw new Gaussian phases, apply the log-normal transform — exactly what a well-trained generative model approximates) to produce 300 realizations, and separately made one deterministic reconstruction by keeping only the 2% largest Fourier coefficients. Then I measured the one-point PDF and the power spectrum of each.

The numbers

The generated realizations reproduce the target's statistics: ensemble variance and a skewed, log-normal one-point PDF (ensemble skewness ) — invariant across realizations even though every sky is different. The deterministic reconstruction instead collapses them: variance falls to and skewness to as the small-scale, non-Gaussian structure is averaged away. Same lesson as the whole note, now made exact for a sky: generation preserves the distribution; reconstruction preserves the specific field, degraded.

Summary

Reconstruction (deterministic AE)Realization (sampled generative model)
Is it the same sky?yes — same structures, blurred no — a different sky
Phaseskept (for retained modes)redrawn at random
Power spectrumsuppressed at small scales preserved (it is what was learned)
One-point PDFnarrowed, pushed toward Gaussian preserved (if the model is non-Gaussian)
Variancereduced ( lost)preserved
What is invariantpositions of retained structures the statistical ensemble

Appendix D — where the variational autoencoder fits

The VAE is the bridge between Appendix C's two operations: it can reconstruct the same sky and generate a new one, with one knob between them.

Appendix C drew a sharp line between reconstruction (same sky, degraded) and realization (new sky, same statistics). A variational autoencoder (VAE) is exactly the model that contains both — and the whole difference is one structural change to the autoencoder of Appendix B.

D.1 — the one change: a probabilistic bottleneck

A plain autoencoder maps to a single code . A VAE's encoder instead outputs a distribution over codes,

— a mean and a spread per latent dimension — and the decoder turns a sampled back into a field. That one change, a spread in the bottleneck, is what lets the same network run in three modes:

Reconstruction
encode, take the posterior mean , decode. This is Appendix C's reconstruction — the same sky, smoothed. In the limit the VAE is an ordinary autoencoder.
Local sampling
draw around the mean and decode — small variations near the input, the uncertain detail resampled.
Generation
ignore the input and draw from the prior, decode — a brand-new realization from the learned distribution: new phases, same statistics.

D.2 — why the ELBO makes generation possible (rate & distortion)

Recall the training objective from §5, now read term by term:

The distortion term wants faithful (same-sky) reconstruction. The rate term pulls every code's distribution toward the prior, which is precisely what makes the latent space samplable: it forces the codes to tile the prior with no gaps, so that a fresh draw from decodes to something realistic. That KL term is the mechanism that turns a compressor into a generator. The of a -VAE is the dial: high → more compression, more generative and smoother; low → sharper reconstruction, less generative. It is the rate–distortion trade-off of §7 made into a training knob.

D.3 — the demonstration

I trained a small convolutional VAE on the same log-normal skies and used it in both modes: I reconstructed a target (posterior mean) and I drew fresh samples from the prior.

The numbers

The samples are genuinely new skies that keep the shape of the distribution (sample skewness vs the true ), but at reduced power (sample variance vs true ; the reconstruction ) — the decoder has blurred away small-scale structure. The VAE has slid us from reconstruction toward generation, and made the characteristic VAE compromise visible.

D.4 — the catch, and the cosmology

That blur is not an accident. A vanilla VAE with a Gaussian (MSE) decoder outputs the conditional mean , so both its reconstructions and its samples tend to be smooth — small-scale power suppressed, the PDF pulled toward Gaussian. This is the same "decoder outputs the mean" effect as in Appendix C, and it is exactly why the lineage runs VAE → expressive decoders → diffusion models, which restore the sharp, non-Gaussian detail.

For weak lensing the VAE therefore sits precisely at the intersection of this note's two threads:

As a compressor
the encoder gives a learned low-dimensional summary of a map — a code you can run inference on (§8), whose size in bits is the rate.
As a generator
sampling the prior is an emulator of mock skies for covariance estimation (§9).
The caveat
a Gaussian-decoder VAE will under-produce the non-Gaussian peaks — the Fisher-information loss of §10. If the science lives in the peaks and the bispectrum, you need the expressive-decoder / diffusion version, or you will generate skies with the right but a flattened PDF.

In one line

A VAE is the autoencoder of Appendix B given a probabilistic bottleneck, which turns it into the generative model of Appendix C — with the ELBO's rate term as the dial between "same sky" and "new sky".

Appendix E — the encoder as stochastic variational inference

"Stochastic variational encoder" is not a separate architecture — it is the VAE encoder, and it names where the VAE's encoder sits in the inference family.

A natural question after Appendix D: is there such a thing as a stochastic variational encoder, and where does it sit? There is — it is precisely the VAE's encoder, also called the inference or recognition network. Two different "stochastic" ideas hide in the name, and both are present at once.

Variational
the encoder outputs an approximate posterior over the code — a variational stand-in for the true, intractable posterior.
Stochastic (latent)
you then sample from it. A plain autoencoder's code is a deterministic point; this one is a distribution you draw from — the "spread in the bottleneck" of Appendix D.
Stochastic (training)
it is fit by stochastic-gradient ascent on the ELBO, with mini-batches and a Monte-Carlo estimate of the expectation — this is the sense in Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI).

E.1 — the VAE is amortized SVI

The umbrella framework is Stochastic Variational Inference (Hoffman, Blei, Wang & Paisley 2013 [12]): fit a variational posterior to huge datasets with noisy mini-batch gradients on the ELBO. The VAE adds one idea on top — amortization:

Classical VI
optimise variational parameters for the whole dataset at once.
SVI
do it with stochastic mini-batch gradients — scalable.
VAE (amortized VI)
instead of re-optimising for every datapoint, an encoder network predicts in a single forward pass. The cost of inference is "amortised" across all datapoints — that network is the stochastic variational encoder.

E.2 — the reparameterization trick makes it trainable

Sampling is not differentiable, so you cannot back-propagate through "draw " directly. The reparameterization trick moves the randomness outside the network:

Now is a deterministic function of (which the encoder produces) and an external noise draw , so gradients flow straight through and . This single trick is what makes the stochastic variational encoder trainable by ordinary back-propagation.

E.3 — where it sits on the inference ladder

Think of a ladder of ways to get the code / posterior, trading accuracy for speed:

MethodEncoderPosteriorCost
Deterministic AEpoint mapnone (a point code)cheapest
VAE = amortized SVIstochastic variational encoder predicted in one passcheap
Per-datapoint SVInone — optimise for each fit by SGDmore accurate, slower
MCMC / exactnonesamples the true posteriormost accurate, slowest

The one-pass encoder is slightly less accurate than optimising afresh for each datapoint — the difference is the amortization gap, and semi-amortized methods (predict with the encoder, then refine with a few SVI steps) close it.

The cosmology parallel

This is exactly the trade-off between a learned summary and full per-field inference in weak lensing. The stochastic variational encoder is the fast, approximate route — one forward pass to a compressed posterior over a map — while per-field SVI or MCMC is the slower gold standard. It is the same VI / SVI machinery from my Bayesian toolkit note, now with a neural encoder bolted on the front to amortise it across every sky in the survey.

Appendix F — latent variables, and "amortized" made simple

What is the hidden "code" everything has been talking about — and what does it really mean that a VAE "amortizes" inference? Two plain answers, with a 1D worked example.

F.1 — what is a latent variable?

A latent variable is a hidden quantity you never measure directly, but which explains or generates what you do measure. The data is the effect; the latent is the cause. The generative story runs one way, inference runs the other:

Everything this note has called the "code" is a latent variable: the PCA coefficients, the autoencoder bottleneck, the VAE's , even MOPED's compressed numbers. It is the compact hidden description of the data. The VAE adds two things that make it a proper probabilistic latent-variable model: a prior on the latent, and an inferred posterior saying which latents could have produced this datum.

Latent variables are everywhere in cosmology

You already work with them constantly. The noise-free convergence field behind the noisy shear is a latent; the cosmological parameters are latents; the initial density field of the Universe, inferred from the CMB or galaxy surveys, is a latent. Inference is the act of recovering latents from data — and a compressed summary is just a low-dimensional latent you have chosen to keep.

F.2 — "inference" means finding the latent for a datum

Given a data point , inference means working out its latent — the distribution . There are two ways to do it, and the difference is the entire meaning of "amortized":

Per-datapoint
for each new , run a little optimization (or MCMC) to find its best . Accurate, but you pay the cost again for every datum.
Amortized
train one encoder function once that outputs for any in a single pass. You learn the rule, not each answer — the cost of inference is "amortized" (spread) across all data.

The analogy: per-datapoint inference is solving each puzzle from scratch; amortized inference is training a solver once and then reading off the answer instantly for any puzzle.

F.3 — a 1D worked example you can check by hand

Take the simplest latent-variable model. A hidden is drawn from a standard Gaussian prior, and the datum is that latent plus noise:

By Bayes' theorem (conjugate Gaussians) the posterior for the latent is itself a Gaussian whose mean is a straight line in :

Put : then and . So for the latent's posterior mean is ; for it is . Now watch the two styles of inference:

Per-datapoint
given , you would iterate an optimizer from some guess until it converges to ; given , iterate again to ; and so on, a fresh optimization for every datum.
Amortized
you instead learn the one number in the rule — training drives . After that, any is answered in one multiplication: . The encoder has learned the line, not the points.

This is exactly why a VAE is called amortized SVI: stochastic variational inference would optimize for each ; the VAE trains an encoder to predict it, paying once to learn the rule and reusing it for the whole dataset.

F.4 — the 2D case is the same idea, scaled up

Nothing changes in principle when the datum is a 2D image. Now the latent is a vector — in the VAE of Appendix D it was 32 numbers — a compact hidden description that the decoder turns into a convergence map. The straight-line rule of the 1D case becomes a nonlinear convolutional encoder, but its job is identical: per-datapoint inference would optimize those 32 latent numbers separately for every map; the amortized encoder of Appendix D spits them out in one forward pass for any map. Feed it a map, and out comes its latent code — no per-map optimization. That trained encoder is the amortization: the cost of inference, learned once, reused for every sky in a survey of billions.

In one line

A latent variable is the hidden code that generates the data; inference is recovering it; and a VAE amortizes that inference by learning one encoder that outputs the latent for any datum in a single step — the 1D line , scaled up to a conv-net that codes a whole sky.

Appendix G — the VAE's ELBO, worked by hand

Everything so far was conceptual or trained. Here the whole VAE objective is computed with a pen in 1D — and it lands exactly on the true posterior.

Take the same tiny latent-variable model as Appendix F: a hidden with a standard-Gaussian prior, and a datum that is the latent plus noise. We will actually evaluate the ELBO and maximise it by hand.

Our approximate posterior is a Gaussian with two numbers to choose, and . The ELBO (§5) is reconstruction minus KL:

G.1 — the reconstruction (distortion) term

With , the expected log-likelihood over is

The only expectation we need is (mean-square = squared bias + variance). So with the reconstruction term is simply — largest when : the reconstruction wants the code to point straight at the datum.

G.2 — the KL (rate) term

For two Gaussians the KL has a closed form you can keep in your head:

This is smallest () when — i.e. when equals the prior. So the rate term wants the code to forget the datum and sit at the prior. The ELBO is the tug-of-war between these two.

And the amortized version (Appendix F) just makes this automatic for every datum: the encoder learns the line , which is the ELBO-maximising for any in one step. The -VAE simply reweights the KL term, , sliding the optimum between "reconstruct" and "match the prior" — the rate–distortion dial of §7, now visible as a shift of the peak in the left panel.

G.4 — the 2D case is the same sum, repeated

Nothing new is needed for a vector latent or a 2D image — the terms just become sums you add up by hand. For a -dimensional diagonal-Gaussian code the KL is a sum of the 1D KLs, and the reconstruction is a sum over pixels:

So a VAE with, say, a 2-number latent and has KL — just the 1D box above, written twice and added. The 2D convergence-map VAE of Appendix D is this exact calculation with latent terms and reconstruction terms: conceptually nothing beyond what you just did with a pen, only more additions.

Appendix H — normalizing flows (and neural-ODE flows)

The exact, invertible cousin of the VAE — and, it turns out, the very thing that generated the log-normal field used all through this note.

A normalizing flow is an invertible map between a simple Gaussian "latent" and the data. Invertible means you can go both ways with no loss: forward turns a Gaussian draw into a data sample; backward turns any datum back into its latent, exactly. The word "normalizing" is literal: the flow learns the transform that turns the data's complicated distribution into a plain normal (Gaussian) one.

H.1 — the one rule: change of variables

If and you know the density of , the density of follows from conservation of probability. Stretch the axis and the density must thin out by the same factor, so that the total still integrates to one:

That slope is the Jacobian — in plain words, how much the map stretches a little interval. In many dimensions it becomes the Jacobian determinant : how much a little box of volume is stretched. A flow is built so this stretch factor is easy to compute, which is what makes the exact log-density available — no bound, unlike the VAE's ELBO.

H.2 — pen-and-paper 1D flow: the log-normal map

Here is the simplest flow of all — and it is the one we have been using since §6. Take a standard-Gaussian latent and exponentiate it:

Invert it: , so the slope is . Plug into the rule:

Check two values by hand: at (), ; at (), . The factor is the Jacobian: as grows the map gets steeper, so it squeezes the probability — which is exactly the long-tailed, skewed log-normal shape.

The punchline

This map is the generator of the log-normal field used throughout the note. "Draw a realization" (Appendices C–G) means run the flow forward (); "encode a field exactly" means run it backward (). A learned flow just replaces the hand-picked with a flexible stack of invertible layers that discovers the right transform from data.

H.3 — the 2D field generator is a flow too

The 2D log-normal convergence maps were made in three steps, and every step is invertible:

1. white noise
draw independent Gaussian numbers (the base latent).
2. colour it
multiply by in Fourier space to imprint the power spectrum — a linear, invertible stretch (divide by to undo it), then an inverse FFT.
3. exponentiate
apply pixel by pixel — the 1D flow above, done everywhere.

So the whole generator is a normalizing flow from white Gaussian noise to the field. And because the log-density is a sum of the log-Jacobians of the steps, you can write it down term by term: the colouring step contributes (one stretch per Fourier mode) and the exponential step contributes (the per pixel). The 2D case is the 1D calculation, added up over modes and pixels — nothing more.

H.4 — flow vs VAE, in plain words

VAENormalizing flow
encoder / decodertwo separate networks one map; the encoder is literally the decoder run backwards
latent sizesmaller than the data (a bottleneck) same size as the data (invertibility needs it)
likelihooda lower bound (the ELBO)exact
reconstructionlossy, blurredperfect (nothing is lost)
samplescan blursharp
compresses?yes (that is the point)no — it trades compression for exactness

In one sentence: a flow never throws anything away, so it reconstructs perfectly and gives an exact likelihood but cannot shrink the data; a VAE shrinks the data but pays with an approximation and some blur. They are two ends of the same encoder–decoder idea.

H.5 — reconstruction, realization, and compression — all exact

Because a flow is invertible it does both operations of Appendix C, exactly: is a perfect, lossless reconstruction (no degradation), and is a new realization with the learned statistics. And since it gives exact , it is directly a lossless compressor in the sense of §9: feed to an arithmetic coder and you hit the entropy floor.

H.6 — "neural flow": the continuous version (neural ODE)

What people often mean by a neural flow is the continuous-time version. Instead of a fixed transform, imagine the point drifting along a learned "current" — a velocity field — and follow it from time to time :

This is a neural ODE / continuous normalizing flow: the transform is the solution of a differential equation whose right-hand side is a small network. The log-density change becomes an integral of the "local stretch rate" (the trace of the Jacobian) along the path. The payoff for us: this is the same object as a diffusion model's probability-flow ODE — so normalizing flows and the diffusion models of the U-Net note are two views of one idea, and both are continuous cousins of the simple map above.

H.7 — where flows sit in cosmology

Flows are the workhorse of simulation-based inference: because they give an exact, flexible density, they are used to model either the posterior over cosmological parameters or the likelihood directly — the final density estimator in the compression→summary→posterior chain of §8. In weak lensing that means flow-based field-level likelihoods , flow posteriors over , and flow emulators of mock maps. And because a flow Gaussianizes, it is the natural learned generalization of the log-transform: it finds the nonlinear map that turns the non-Gaussian, phase-correlated field into independent Gaussian latents — the deep-learning counterpart of the phase statistics in my own work.

In one line

A normalizing flow is an invertible transform that Gaussianizes the data; the log-normal field's is the one-line example; it reconstructs perfectly and gives an exact likelihood (so it is a perfect compressor-and-generator), and its continuous "neural ODE" form is the same thing as a diffusion model.

Appendix I — the neighbourhood: fields related to compression

A one-line map of the topics that sit next to data compression — seeds to develop later.

Compression is really the question "what is the shortest honest description of this data?", so it touches most fields that deal with information, inference or structure. A pointer to each:

Information theory — the parent field

Channel coding / error-correcting codes
the mirror of compression: add redundancy cleverly so a message survives noise (Shannon's second theorem).
Mutual information, KL divergence, cross-entropy
the currencies that measure shared information, model mismatch, and code length.
Kolmogorov complexity / algorithmic information
the length of the shortest program that outputs the data — the ultimate, uncomputable compressor (Solomonoff induction).
Asymptotic equipartition / typical sets
why long data streams concentrate on a tiny "typical" set of size — the reason entropy is the compression floor.

Statistics & inference

MDL & model selection (BIC, AIC, Bayesian evidence)
"the model that compresses best wins" — BIC is essentially MDL; the Occam factor penalises complexity in bits.
Maximum-entropy principle (Jaynes)
the flip side of compression: the least-committal distribution consistent with what you know — and the bridge to statistical mechanics.
Sufficient statistics / Fisher / Cramér–Rao
the "keep the information" half: the smallest summary that loses no information about the parameters.
Compressed sensing / sparse coding
recover a signal from far fewer measurements than Nyquist if it is sparse in some basis — transform coding turned into a measurement strategy.

Signal processing

Sampling theorem (Nyquist–Shannon)
how few samples capture a band-limited signal exactly — the first "compression" most physicists meet.
Quantization / vector quantization
rounding coefficients to a finite codebook (-means / Lloyd's algorithm; VQ-VAE brings it into modern generative models and tokenization).
Wavelets / DCT / Fourier transforms
the sparsifying bases that make lossy compression (JPEG, JPEG 2000) and mass-map denoising work.

Machine learning

PCA
decorrelate and keep the top-variance directions — the optimal linear compressor (§3).
ICA (independent component analysis)
go beyond PCA: find statistically independent sources, not just uncorrelated ones — needs non-Gaussianity, used for source separation (e.g. CMB foreground cleaning / SMICA).
Manifold learning (t-SNE, UMAP, autoencoders)
find compact, possibly curved coordinates for high-dimensional data.
Information bottleneck
learning as compressing the input while keeping what is relevant to a target (§7).
Model compression (pruning, quantization, distillation)
a different axis — shrink the network, not the data, into a small one that behaves the same.
Generalization ↔ compression (PAC-Bayes, MDL bounds)
a model that compresses its training data tends to generalise — Occam's razor with a theorem attached.

Physics — the deepest connections

Thermodynamic entropy ↔ Shannon entropy
Jaynes showed statistical mechanics is maximum-entropy inference — the same entropy, two guises.
Landauer's principle / Maxwell's demon
erasing one bit costs at least of energy — the physical price of information, tying computation to the second law.
Renormalization group as coarse-graining
integrating out small scales to keep the relevant large-scale physics is compression; a known analogy to the layers of a deep network.

Cosmology — your domain

MOPED / Karhunen–Loève compression
compress a huge data vector to one number per parameter while preserving the Fisher information (§3–4).
Summary statistics as compression
power spectrum, bispectrum, peak counts, morphology — each a physically chosen lossy compression of the field (§8).
Wavelet scattering transforms
a powerful modern compression for non-Gaussian fields — a natural neighbour of the bispectrum and phase statistics.
Emulators & simulation-based inference
compressing expensive simulations and likelihoods into fast surrogate models and learned posteriors (§8–9).

One way to see the whole map: compression removes redundancy, error-correction adds it to beat noise, maximum-entropy finds the least description consistent with constraints, the renormalization group throws away the description you do not need, and sufficient statistics / MOPED keep only the description that carries the parameters — all the same question, asked from different sides.

Appendix J — ICA as whitening + a rotation

PCA is an eigenvalue problem; ICA is PCA plus the one extra rotation that second-order statistics cannot fix. Here it is, with a 2D pen-and-paper example.

Recall the contrast with PCA. PCA maximises the variance of a projection, a quadratic form, so it is the eigenproblem . ICA instead starts from a generative model: the data is a linear mixture of unknown, independent, non-Gaussian sources,

and we want the unmixing matrix so that has independent components. The clean way to solve it is in two steps.

J.1 — Step 1: whiten (this is exactly PCA)

Transform the data so its covariance becomes the identity, using the eigen-decomposition :

Pen-and-paper: whitening a 2×2 covariance

Take . The characteristic equation gives , with eigenvectors and . Whitening is then: rotate into this eigenbasis, scale each axis by (so by and ), and rotate back — . That is all second-order information, and it is pure PCA, done by hand.

J.2 — Step 2: the leftover rotation

Here is the crux. Whitening does not finish the job, because any rotation of whitened data is still whitened: for an orthogonal , . Covariance is blind to this rotation. So the true unmixing must have the form

and the only thing ICA adds beyond PCA is finding that rotation . In 2D it is a single angle .

J.3 — What fixes the rotation: maximum non-Gaussianity

Independence is measured by the mutual information . Since a rotation preserves and the have unit variance, minimising mutual information is exactly maximising the non-Gaussianity of each component. So ICA solves

with a non-Gaussianity measure — most simply the squared excess kurtosis (which is for a Gaussian), or the negentropy that FastICA uses. The intuition is the central limit theorem: a mixture of independent variables is more Gaussian than the sources, so the most non-Gaussian projections are the sources. Because non-Gaussianity is a fourth-and-higher-order functional, not a quadratic form, there is no eigen-equation — you find by iterative optimisation (a grid search in 2D, FastICA in general).

J.4 — Two things to remember

Indeterminacies
ICA recovers the sources only up to permutation (which source is which) and sign / scale — non-Gaussianity and independence say nothing about order or amplitude.
The Gaussian failure
if the sources are Gaussian, every rotation of whitened data is equally Gaussian, so is undetermined and ICA collapses to PCA. ICA has content only where the data is non-Gaussian — which is exactly why it is a natural tool in non-Gaussian cosmology (e.g. CMB component separation / SMICA), and a cousin of higher-order statistics.

In one line

PCA = "diagonalise the covariance" (an eigenvalue problem, second order); ICA = "whiten, then rotate to make the components as non-Gaussian / independent as possible" (PCA plus a higher-order rotation that has no eigen-solution).

Reproducibility. The demo simulates non-Gaussian (log-normal) weak-lensing convergence maps, then compresses them with PCA (SVD of the training set), undecimated-wavelet top- thresholding, and a convolutional autoencoder trained from scratch (PyTorch), measuring both reconstruction RMSE and recovered skewness versus compression ratio. Every figure and number comes from that single script.
